A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ChatInject study. All 24 pages of v1 and 28 pages of v2, including their figures, tables, equations and appendices, support comparison; relocated and renumbered material can be matched.

before.justification: v1 reports original attack-success and utility measurements on AgentDojo and InjecAgent, together with transferability, defense and perturbation experiments.

after.justification: v2 retains these original experiments and adds corpus comparisons, attention measurements, homoglyph tests and further defense-related results.

M1.justification: The four payload variants, GPT-4.1 dialogue-generation procedure, reasoning/tool hooks and mixture-of-templates construction are retained. The stronger emphasis on simulated dialogue clarifies the existing method; the added appendix experiments do not revise its procedure.

E1.justification: AgentDojo's Slack, travel and banking domains and InjecAgent's attack tasks remain unchanged. Appendix C.1 adds human jailbreak dialogues from Li et al. (2024), adapted into tool-directed injection attacks, while C.4 adds a Unicode-homoglyph input scenario.

E2.justification: Figure 5 adds Lakera Guard alongside the four retained defenses. New Table 3 compares adapted human attack dialogues against the synthetic persuasion dialogues, and Table 8 adds a Claude-system-prompt condition on existing models; Claude itself is not added as an evaluated backbone.

E3.justification: The principal benchmarks, model roster, ASR/utility metrics and temperature-0 setup remain unchanged. Added analyses introduce last-input-token attention measurements, GPT-4.1 adaptation of human dialogues, homoglyph encoding and system-prompt substitution. Newly disclosed benchmark sample counts do not establish a change to existing samples.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained turn-count, persuasion, template-mixing and perturbation analyses, v2 tests synthetic versus adapted human dialogues, attention allocation between user and attacker instructions, sensitivity to homoglyph encoding, and whether Claude's system prompt preserves utility. These substantially expand the investigation of mechanism, realism and failure conditions.

E5.justification: v1 already reports five-seed means and standard deviations for template mixing and perturbations. v2 extends uncertainty reporting to the principal results through 95% Wilson intervals in Figures 3 and 5 and Appendix E, Tables 10–11. These quantify finite-sample uncertainty rather than documenting additional repeated runs.

E6.justification: Table 1 and the original result cells of Table 2 retain their values, while Table 2 gains averages. Substantial new findings include adapted-human versus synthetic ASRs of 76.3/80.5% for Qwen-3 and 27.5/48.1% for GLM-4.5, increased attacker attention in Table 5, and homoglyph ASRs of 17.5%, 0.3% and 1.5% for Qwen-3, GPT-oss and Llama-4. Figure 5 and Table 8 add detector and system-prompt results under new conditions.

T1.justification: Section 3.1 newly makes explicit that the attacker cannot access the user instruction or internal prompts and can manipulate only tool-response content. The existing dialogue formulation and embedding-similarity equations remain unchanged; no theorems or proofs are added.

C1.justification: The central claims about attack effectiveness, cross-model transfer and weaknesses of existing defenses remain unchanged, as do the abstract's headline numerical results and the conclusion. The introduction clarifies that multi-turn dialogue is simulated within one injection, which was already represented by v1's method and examples.

C2.justification: v2 adds an attention-based explanation of template authority, a similarity-preservation qualification for alternative encodings, and an explanation linking detector utility loss to removal of entire tool outputs. It revises the closed-model utility discussion using the inconclusive Claude-prompt experiment and adds interpretations concerning dialogue realism and utility metrics. Appendix B nevertheless retains its now-conflicting statement that attention analysis was unavailable.

D1.justification: v2 newly documents benchmark sample counts of 389 and 1054, hook eligibility, human-dialogue adaptation and review, attention measurement steps, and Lakera's external-API role. Existing provider lists, decoding settings, generation prompts and model-specific tags are retained. The repository link is relocated without establishing a change in resource availability.

R1.justification: Section 2 expands its treatment of instruction hierarchy and simulated versus interactive multi-turn attacks, adding references including Greshake, Zverev and Rahman. Additional citations support the new corpus, attention, homoglyph, detector and statistical analyses. The fundamental positioning against plain-text injection and ChatBug remains intact.

P1.justification: The introduction's multi-turn explanation and related-work section are locally rewritten, with related work organized into three thematic paragraphs. Appendix subsections and confidence-interval cross-references are added, and publication headers change. Most existing prose and the sequence of main Sections 1–7 are retained.

P2.justification: v2 substantially expands the empirical displays with new analysis tables and confidence-interval counterparts of the main tables. Table 2 gains average rows and a column; Figure 3 gains confidence bands, and Figure 5 is redrawn with Lakera Guard and uncertainty bars. Other figures and prompt tables are retained, sometimes relocated.

improvement.justification: Wilson intervals and the added corpus, encoding and defense controls make the existing findings' uncertainty and applicability easier to assess. The gains are limited by strong mechanistic and realism interpretations of narrow tests and reporting inconsistencies: Appendix B still denies attention analysis despite C.3, and Table 8 labels utility results as ASR. Overall, v2 provides useful additional support without fully resolving these explanatory and reporting weaknesses.
